mean: to learn a fact or the truth, often by asking or checking
ex: Can you find out what time the last bus leaves Varanasi for Prayagraj on Sunday?
note: 'I came to know' is common in India; 'I found out' sounds more natural elsewhere. Say 'find out about it'.
ex2: Shiv used the hospital app to find out whether his blood test reports were ready.

mean: to stop trying, or to stop a habit
ex: Arjun refused to give up even after failing the CA final twice.
note: Separable: 'give it up', never 'give up it'. Use -ing after it: 'give up eating sugar'. 'Give up on someone' = stop hoping.
ex2: The doctor told Mr Gill to give up smoking after the scan showed damage to his lungs.

mean: to examine a problem or complaint to find out the facts
ex: The railway helpline promised to look into my complaint about the broken AC in coach B3.
note: Not separable: 'look into it', never 'look it into'. 'I'll look into it' is a polite office promise, so do follow it up.
ex2: The principal agreed to look into why the school canteen was charging extra for samosas.

mean: to make someone notice a fact, often a mistake
ex: Thanks for taking the time to point out the error in the GST figure before the invoice went out.
note: Separable: 'point it out'. A common pattern is 'point out that...'. Softer than 'correct': 'May I point out one thing?'
ex2: During the Ranji match, the coach was quick to point out the gap the bowlers kept leaving at mid-wicket.

mean: to start talking about a subject
ex: Please don't bring up the property dispute at Nani's birthday lunch; everyone will start shouting.
note: Separable: 'bring it up'. Second meaning: to raise a child ('She was brought up in Patna').
ex2: At the parent-teacher meeting, Mrs Das decided to bring up the problem of heavy school bags.

mean: to continue doing something
ex: Sorry for the interruption, Professor Iyer; please carry on with the lecture.
note: Mostly spoken; in formal writing 'continue' is better. Use 'carry on + -ing' or 'carry on with + noun'.
ex2: The power went off during the sangeet, but the dhol players decided to carry on in the dark.

mean: to find or meet by chance; also, to seem a certain way
ex: If you come across a good tailor in Lajpat Nagar, please send me the number.
note: Two meanings: find by chance ('come across an old letter') and seem ('He comes across as arrogant'). Not separable.
ex2: While cleaning Nanaji's almirah, I happened to come across letters he wrote from Assam in 1962.

mean: to understand or solve something after thinking about it
ex: Priya spent the whole evening trying to figure out why the hostel Wi-Fi kept disconnecting.
note: Casual but fine at work. Separable: 'figure it out'. 'Work out' means the same and sounds more British.
ex2: Sanjay could not figure out the new tax portal, so he asked his daughter to help him file the return.

mean: to delay doing something until later
ex: Stop trying to put off the dentist visit, Rahul; that tooth won't fix itself.
note: Separable: 'put it off'. Also means 'make someone dislike': 'His rudeness put me off.' 'Postpone' is the formal word.
ex2: Many students put off revision until the last week before the boards, and then they panic.

mean: to say no to an offer, request or invitation
ex: It was hard to turn down a job in Dubai, but Faisal wanted to stay near his parents in Lucknow.
note: Separable: 'turn it down', never 'turn down it'. Also means lower the volume: 'turn the TV down'. 'Reject' sounds harsher.
ex2: Meera decided to turn down the marriage proposal her uncle brought from Indore.

mean: to decide that something is not possible or not the cause
ex: The doctor ordered a blood test to rule out dengue before treating the fever as viral.
note: Very common in news: 'Police have not ruled out foul play.' Separable: 'rule it out'.
ex2: The weather office did not rule out heavy rain in Mumbai during Ganpati visarjan.

mean: to support a claim with proof, or to support a person
ex: If you say sales fell because of the rains, back up the claim with numbers from each district.
note: Also means to copy computer data. The verb is two words (back up); the noun is one (a backup).
ex2: When the shopkeeper denied overcharging, two other customers were ready to back up Leela's story.

mean: to fix a problem or put things in order
ex: Let me sort out the seating plan before the baraat arrives.
note: Friendly and common in British and Indian speech. Separable: 'sort it out'. 'Sorted!' means everything is fixed.
ex2: Ravi spent his Saturday at the bank trying to sort out a mistake in his home loan statement.

mean: to start or arrange something, such as a business, meeting or system
ex: My cousin Joseph left his bank job to set up a cloud kitchen in Pune.
note: Verb: two words (set up). Noun: 'a setup' or 'a set-up'. 'Set someone up' can also mean trick them into looking guilty.
ex2: The panchayat plans to set up a small library in the old school building.

mean: to think of an idea, plan or answer
ex: The team has two days to come up with a cheaper design for the solar water pump.
note: Cannot be split: 'come up with it', never 'come it up with'. Use it for new ideas; 'devise' is the formal version.
ex2: My niece in Class 6 managed to come up with a clever science project using old plastic bottles.

mean: to finish what you started or promised
hi: बात पूरी करना, अंजाम तक पहुँचाना
ex: Many people announce a fitness plan on New Year's Day; few follow through after the first week.
note: Not 'follow up' (check again later): follow through = actually complete it. In cricket, the follow-through is the end of the bowling action.
ex2: The coach said talent is useless unless you follow through on your training plan every single day.

mean: to make something seem less important or serious than it is
ex: The airline tried to play down the delay, but passengers had been stuck at Chennai airport for six hours.
note: Opposite: 'play up'. Separable: 'play it down'. Common in news: 'Officials played down fears of a shortage.' Also one word: 'downplay'.
ex2: The team doctor tried to play down the captain's knee injury, but he missed the next two matches.

mean: to refuse to take something seriously or to listen to it
ex: Don't brush off a chest pain as gas, Papa; get an ECG done today.
note: Separable: 'brush it off'. It hints at carelessness. 'Give someone the brush-off' = rudely reject them.
ex2: Shreya's boss tends to brush off her ideas in meetings, then presents them as his own a week later.

mean: to be as good as people expected
ex: The new biryani place in Hyderabad did not live up to the hype on Instagram.
note: Here 'live' rhymes with 'give', not 'five'. Cannot be split. Often negative: 'failed to live up to'.
ex2: As the topper's younger brother, Aman felt he could never live up to the family's hopes.

mean: (of a plan or deal) to fail and not happen
hi: बात न बनना, खटाई में पड़ना
ex: Get the agreement in writing, or the flat deal may fall through at the last minute.
with: fall through at the last minute
note: Used for plans and deals, not people: 'The deal fell through.' It takes no object.
ex2: Our family trip to Darjeeling may fall through if Papa doesn't get leave from the bank.

mean: to become popular; also, to finally understand
ex: Nobody expected UPI to catch on so fast among sabziwalas and chai stalls.
note: Two senses: become popular ('the trend caught on') and understand ('she caught on to the trick'). Casual but fine at work.
ex2: Some dialogues from new films catch on so fast that every college canteen is repeating them within a week.

mean: to pass quickly over a problem so that people don't notice it
ex: The annual report seems to gloss over the losses in the Kolkata branch.
note: Always critical: it suggests hiding something. Not split in normal use: 'gloss over it'.
ex2: The wedding planner tried to gloss over the extra charges, but Mr Ghosh read every line of the bill.

mean: to solve small problems or differences before things go ahead
ex: The two families met over chai to iron out the last details of the wedding budget.
note: Picture pressing creases flat. Used for small problems, not big crises. Separable: 'iron them out'. Say EYE-urn, not 'eye-RON'.
ex2: The startup and its Japanese investor need a week to iron out the last details of the deal.

mean: to give your opinion in a discussion, often as an expert
ex: Before we finalise the leave policy, I'd like Meenakshi from legal to weigh in.
note: Fine at work and in news. Use 'on' + topic: 'weigh in on the debate'. Not separable.
ex2: In our family WhatsApp group, everyone wanted to weigh in on what Chhotu should study after Class 12.

mean: to think carefully about something for a while before deciding
ex: Take the weekend to mull over the offer from the Bengaluru startup before you reply.
instead: think about it for some time
note: Separable: 'mull it over'. It suggests slow, unhurried thinking.
ex2: Grandma likes to mull over the crossword clues with her tea before she writes a single answer.

mean: to stick to a choice even more firmly after people question it
ex: Instead of apologising, the anchor chose to double down on his claim in the next night's debate.
note: From card games (doubling a bet). American, now common in news. Usually critical (stubbornness), but can be positive: 'double down on quality'.
ex2: When the new rule on hostel timings drew protests, the warden chose to double down and make it even stricter.

mean: to develop or end in a particular way
ex: Nobody knows how the Ranji season will pan out now that three key players are injured.
note: Casual. Often negative or uncertain: 'The plan didn't pan out.' From gold miners washing gravel in a pan.
ex2: If the mango crop doesn't pan out this summer, the Patils will have to borrow money again.

mean: to feel happy and excited about something that will happen
ex: The children in our Kochi building look forward to Onam all year because of the sadya and the boat races.
with: look forward to hearing from you
note: Follow it with a noun or -ing: 'look forward to meeting you', never 'look forward to meet you'.
ex2: Nurses on night duty at the district hospital look forward to the 3 a.m. chai break more than anything else.

mean: to use all of something so that none is left
ex: We stopped at a dhaba near Panipat because the car was about to run out of petrol.
note: Indians often say 'the milk got over'; 'we ran out of milk' or 'the milk ran out' is clear everywhere.
ex2: Ask your question quickly, because the speaker at the Kolkata book fair will soon run out of time.

mean: to cancel a plan or event
ex: The school had to call off sports day because heavy monsoon rain flooded the ground.
note: Separable: 'call it off', never 'call off it'. Newspapers love it: unions 'call off' a strike.
ex2: The transport union agreed to call off the strike after talks with officials late on Tuesday night.

mean: to accept something annoying without complaining
ex: How do you put up with the drilling from the flat upstairs at seven every morning, Farhan?
note: Indians often say 'adjust with it'; 'put up with it' is the natural phrase. Never 'put up it'.
ex2: Commuters on the Virar fast local put up with heat, crowds and delays because there is no quicker way to work.

mean: to use or do less of something
ex: The doctor told Mr Bhatia to cut down on salt and fried snacks after his blood pressure reading.
note: 'Cut down on sugar' means eat less of it; 'cut out sugar' means stop it completely.
ex2: To save money for her MBA, Anjali decided to cut down on food orders and cook in the hostel kitchen.

mean: to admire and respect someone as an example
ex: Young players at the Ranchi academy look up to the senior wicketkeeper for his calm under pressure.
with: a person to look up to
note: Opposite: 'look down on' someone, which means thinking they are worse than you.
ex2: Girls in the village look up to Lakshmi, the first person from there to become a doctor.

mean: to feel better after an illness, a shock or a sad event
ex: It took Imran months to get over the loss of his grandfather's shop in the floods.
note: In Indian English 'the exam got over' means it ended; globally 'get over' means to recover from something.
ex2: Cricket fans in Ahmedabad took weeks to get over the World Cup final defeat.

mean: to have something as its main or most basic point
ex: All the arguments about the new metro line boil down to one question: who will pay for it?
note: Usually said as 'it all boils down to...'. Fine at work and in speech.
ex2: For most families choosing a school in Lucknow, the decision will boil down to fees and distance.

mean: to explain something clearly and in full detail
ex: The new manager in Noida took time to spell out exactly what she expected from each person on the team.
note: 'Do I have to spell it out for you?' sounds sharp, even rude, so use it carefully.
ex2: The panchayat notice did not spell out who would get the new handpumps, so villagers crowded the sarpanch's office.

mean: to defend a person or an idea when others attack it
ex: When seniors mocked his accent, Tenzing's roommate was the only one to stand up for him.
note: 'Stand up for' means defend; 'stand up to' means face a bully or a powerful person bravely.
ex2: Grandma taught us to stand up for the truth, even if the whole mohalla disagreed.

mean: to decide not to do something you had agreed to do
ex: The main sponsor chose to back out of the college fest just two days before the opening night.
with: back out at the last minute
note: Say 'back out of' the deal. Do not confuse it with 'back up', which means to support.
ex2: Never back out of a promise to your little sister; she will remind you of it at every Raksha Bandhan.

mean: to stop using something slowly, in planned stages
ex: Delhi plans to phase out old diesel buses and replace them with electric ones over five years.
note: The opposite is 'phase in'. Common in news, business and policy writing.
ex2: Our grocery store in Thrissur will phase out plastic bags by Onam and sell cloth bags at the counter.

mean: to include something when you plan or calculate
ex: When you plan the Manali trip budget, factor in the cost of snow boots and taxi rides.
note: Fine at work, especially for plans and numbers. You can also say 'factor it in'.
ex2: Engineers on the Mumbai coastal road had to factor in high tides and monsoon storms.

mean: to go on for much longer than needed, in a tiring way
ex: If the review meeting continues to drag on, we will miss the 6:15 local from Dadar.
note: Used for meetings, court cases, speeches and disputes. Neutral and fine in news writing.
ex2: Property cases can drag on in district courts for decades, so Mr Kulkarni chose to settle with his cousin.

mean: to hide a problem quickly instead of really solving it
ex: A free dinner for staff cannot paper over the fact that salaries have been late for three months.
note: Usually 'paper over the cracks'. Common in editorials; it suggests the fix is only on the surface.
ex2: A smiling group photo at Diwali cannot paper over the quarrel between the two brothers who share the shop.

mean: to support or strengthen something that is weak or failing
ex: The bank raised fresh money to shore up its finances after heavy losses on bad loans.
note: From the wooden props, called shores, that hold up a weak wall. Common in business and political news.
ex2: Villagers piled sandbags to shore up the river bank before the Brahmaputra rose again.
